title: The video is ready. The first line is what stopped you.
markdown:
# The video is ready. The first line is what stopped you.

At 9:18 p.m., the clips are trimmed, the room looks right, and the edit already has a beat. You open your notes app to write the voiceover. The cursor blinks long enough to make the whole video feel silly. A video you could picture an hour ago now needs a hook, a reason to keep watching, and words that do not sound borrowed.

If that is where your TikToks stall, the problem is not that you cannot make video. It is that a blank page is asking you to make too many decisions at once. This article gives you a smaller job: turn footage and one real moment into a script you can say out loud.

## Begin with the thing that happened

Do not start with a category. "A TikTok about meal prep" gives you no sentence to write. Start with the moment that made the video worth making.

Write this in plain language:

> I made this because [something specific happened], and I wanted [a specific result].

For example: "I made this because I kept buying lunch when food was already in my fridge, and I wanted five lunches ready before Monday."

That is not your finished hook. It is a point of view. It tells you what the video is about before you start trying to sound clever.

## Give the opening one job

The first line only needs to help the right viewer recognize the problem. It does not need to promise a viral transformation.

Compare these:

"Here are some tips for meal prep."

"If lunch keeps costing you money because the food at home needs too much thinking, make this on Sunday."

The second line has a person in it, a frustration, and a reason to stay. Your footage can prove the rest. Before you record, ask one question: would someone who has this problem know the next seconds are for them?

## Use the footage to choose the middle

Writing becomes much easier when the clips get a vote. Lay out what you already shot and name what each clip shows: the overstuffed drawer, the failed attempt, the close-up that explains the fix, the result on the counter.

Then give each useful clip a sentence that adds something the image cannot. A shot of you chopping onions does not need the line "I am chopping onions." It might need: "I stopped preparing every vegetable at once because the herbs were soft by Wednesday."

The video handles the obvious action. The script supplies the choice, the reason, or the small surprise. If a line merely narrates what viewers can see, cut it.

## Keep the structure short enough to film

A practical short script often has three moves:

1. Name the friction.
2. Show the change you made.
3. Leave the viewer with the result or next step.

For a small-kitchen video, that might be: "I kept pulling out half this cabinet to find one pan. I moved the tools I use every day to this shelf. Now dinner starts without the metal avalanche."

It is not poetry, and that is useful. You can point a camera at every part of it. If the middle keeps wandering, return to the question your first line raised and cut anything that does not answer it.

## Write a rough version before you improve it

Trying to make the first pass sound natural can trap you in revisions before there is anything to revise. Draft the hook, the three moves, and one line for each clip. Read it aloud once. Shorten the words that catch in your mouth. Replace polished phrases you would never say with the wording you use when explaining the same thing to a friend.

The goal is not a script that could belong to any creator. It is a usable draft that fits your footage and gives you something concrete to change.

## When you need a starting draft

Sometimes you have the clips and the point but still cannot make the first sentence arrive. Give TikTok Script Pro the topic, who the video is for, the footage you have, and any phrasing you would avoid. Its example output for a 30-second video about cold email starts with a recommended hook and follows it with a beat-by-beat Hook, Build, Payoff, and CTA script. Treat that as a first pass, then keep only the lines that are true for your video and sound like something you would say.

[Try TikTok Script Pro for your next script draft.](https://capafy.ai/agent/2844813315?ct=tiktok_blog)

## A blank page is not a verdict on your idea

The camera work was never the whole job. A script gives the viewer a path through the footage, and it gives you a reason to press record instead of reopening the notes app tomorrow.

Start with the moment that happened. Let the clips decide what needs explaining. Get a rough version on the page. Then make it yours.
